groups.heading: OPTIONAL SOURCE DEPTH
items: Early Orientalist policy supported institutions like Calcutta Madrasa and Sanskrit College ,
reflecting an attempt to govern through classical learning and traditional elites.
The Anglicist victory after Macaulay's Minute and Bentinck's 1835 resolution shifted state support toward English education and Western knowledge.
The downward filtration theory assumed that educating a small English-educated elite would spread knowledge to the wider population.

groups.heading: ADVANCED DEBATE
items: Wood's Despatch, 1854 broadened the framework by recommending a department of public
instruction in each province, grants-in-aid, teacher training, vernacular primary education and universities.
CAUTION: English education served colonial administrative needs, but it also produced the
intelligentsia that criticised colonial rule using liberal, rationalist and nationalist arguments.

groups.heading: LEGACY / NUANCE
items: The Indian press began with Hicky's Bengal Gazette (1780) and expanded into English and vernacular spaces of debate.
Metcalfe's 1835 press policy earned him the title "liberator of the press", but later crises produced restrictions such as the Licensing Act of 1857.
Vernacular Press Act, 1878 under Lytton targeted Indian-language newspapers; Amrita Bazar Patrika famously shifted to English to escape its scope.
